newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac slams left, appeals for support.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac slams left, appeals for support.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac waded into France's tight parliamentary election race on Wednesday with a frontal assault on the record and proposals of the left-wing opposition and an appeal for voters' trust and support.

In an article in 14 regional newspapers marking the second anniversary of his election, the conservative president urged the French people not to turn their backs on history in the snap poll he has called for May 25 and June 1.
Accusing the left of wasteful tax-and-spend policies, Chirac urged voters to cast their ballots for the "political stability indispensible for effective action".
"I need your support to continue the work we have begun together and which can only bear fruit over time. Let's seize our opportunity in a shared elan," he said.

Opinion polls published on Tuesday showed a massive 65 percent of voters were disappointed with Chirac's two years in office and felt his record was negative. A crushing 87 percent said his action had been negative in fighting unemployment.
Yet Chirac, seeking to give his flagging centre-right coalition a second wind, blamed the left for all France's ills.
He said the country had not always made the right choices and cited inefficient spending, a bloated public sector and high taxes, payroll charges and public debt.

Without mentioning unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe, he said the coalition elected in 1993 had been obliged to "wipe the slate clean" before making a new start, arguing that the economy was now cleaned up and growth was returning.

Assailing the left's platform, he said: "Will we bring down unemployment by decree or creating ever more public sector jobs?...On the eve of the 21st century, how can one imagine an authoritarian reduction in the working week, on the same day in every French company?"
The Socialists and Communists have promised to create 700,000 youth jobs, half of them in the public sector, and cut the work week to 35 hours from 39 within three years.
Chirac sprinkled his appeal with buzzwords, some apparently borrowed from Britain's new Prime Minister Tony Blair and U.S. President Bill Clinton, such as "trust" and the 21st century.
He made specific pitches to voter groups alienated from the government such as the medical profession, women and the young.
Ignoring political funding scandals lapping at the heels of his own party, the president pointed to financial scandals and huge losses at public companies managed by the Socialists.
Chirac phrased his article as an explicit appeal to voters to renew confidence in him two years after he took office.

The message took the same form as the announcement of his 1995 presidential candidacy, when he announced his decision to stand in an article in regional newspapers intended to go over the heads of media executives and address voters directly.
Opposition leaders, neck-and-neck with the centre-right in voting intentions according to opinion polls, dismissed Chirac's intervention in advance.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said the momentum was now with the left and there was nothing Chirac could say that would change the course of events.
"They thought they could surprise the French people, catch the opposition napping and wrap up the election before it had even started," Jospin told a rally in Nantes, western France.
"But nothing is wrapped up. On the contrary, this little obstacle on the course called the French people could very well trip them up," he said.

The latest in a daily flood of polls, taken by the CSA institute for Le Parisien daily, gave the combined left 41.5 percent of the vote, the centre-right 40.5, the extreme-right National Front 13.5 and ecologists 4.5 percent.

But it suggested the coalition would retain a National Assembly majority, winning 301 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France to 232 for the Socialists, 21 for the Communists and one for the National Front.
In the outgoing parliament, the coalition held most of the 22 seats in France's overseas territories, which were not covered by the poll.
